theory.text: Every time you solve an interesting problem with the AI, you're about to lose something. The approach you found — the precise prompt, the structure that worked, the sequence that produced the right result — vanishes into the chat. Next time you hit the same problem, you start from scratch. The most productive vibe coders don't work that way: they accumulate patterns. Every working solution becomes a reusable template for the next project.

The fastest way to build the library is reverse meta-prompting: after solving a problem, ask the AI to abstract it. "Summarize what we did and generate a reusable prompt template for doing the same thing in another project." The AI produces a template with placeholders — [STACK], [ENTITY], [CONSTRAINT] — that you paste into your library and adapt in seconds. You don't have to think about it: it does it for you.

theory.prompt: We just implemented magic link authentication with Supabase. Generate a reusable prompt template for doing the same thing in future projects, with placeholders for the variables.
theory.output:
Prompt template — Magic link auth:

"Implement magic link authentication. Stack: [FRAMEWORK] + [AUTH_PROVIDER]. Redirect to [REDIRECT_PATH] after login. DO NOT touch [FILE_NOT_TO_TOUCH]. Code only, one comment per function."

Placeholders: FRAMEWORK, AUTH_PROVIDER, REDIRECT_PATH, FILE_NOT_TO_TOUCH.

theory.text: 💡 Organize the library by category, not by project: Initial setup, Debug, Refactor, Code review, Documentation, Tests. Cross-cutting categories work on any codebase — project-specific ones almost never do.

In 2025-2026, an unexpected phenomenon exploded on YouTube: people started selling their prompt libraries and AGENTS.md files as products. Dedicated channels compare cursor rules like synthesizer presets — some battle-tested pattern packs rack up thousands of downloads. It's not just a trend: it's confirmation that a good pattern library has real, transferable value. The time you invest in building it doesn't just help you.

A poorly maintained library is worse than no library at all. Templates written in a rush, never tested on a second project, give a false sense of security. Keep it small and verified: ten templates that always work beat fifty that sometimes do. Every pattern you add should have already saved at least half an hour on a real project.
🔑 After every interesting problem solved, thirty seconds: "Generate a reusable prompt template for this." It's the highest effort-to-return ratio action in the entire course.

outro.recap: A pattern library is the most underrated productivity multiplier in vibe coding: every template you build today saves time on every future project.
outro.next_prompt: You've completed Path 2. You now have the tools to build anything — one prompt at a time.
